title: Ruling 2023-03: Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement (ICHRA) Qualifies as "Health Care Coverage"
text:
Date: August 28, 2023

Written by: Emily Bergquist

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your company, [Taxpayer], Taxpayer, regarding whether an Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement qualifies as an offer of insurance for the purposes of the Health Care Fund Contribution Assessment. This ruling is based upon representations in your request letter received in this office [date].

Facts 

Your company proposes to offer an Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement for its employees. You ask whether this plan will qualify as “health care coverage” for purposes of your company’s employer liability under Vermont’s Health Care Fund contribution law. You have also asked for directions on completing the Department’s Health Care reporting forms.

Discussion 

Vermont law provides generally that an employer who does not offer “health care coverage” to its employees must pay a “Health Care Fund contribution” for each “uncovered employee” in excess of four employees. 32 V.S.A. § 10503(a).

You have asked whether an Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement (ICHRA) qualifies as “health care coverage” for purposes of the Health Care Fund contribution law.

Under an ICHRA, an employer reimburses its employees for a portion of their health care costs. To qualify as an ICHRA, the plan must meet the requirements of the Federal ICHRA provisions. See, Health Reimbursement Arrangements and Other Account-Based Group Health Plans, 84 FR 28888-01, 2019 WL 2524535(F.R.).

“Health care coverage” is defined in the Vermont statute as “any private or public plan that includes both hospital and physician services.” 32 V.S.A. § 10502(4). There is no further definition of “health care coverage” in the statute. The Department of Taxes (Department) has stated in its publication “Guide to the Health Care Fund Contribution Assessment” that the health care coverage law “requires an employer to pay for part of a plan but does not specify how much it must pay. Thus, any amount paid by the employer is acceptable for an employee to be considered covered.” Id., p. 4. The only other statutory requirement is that the “plan” that is paid for must provide coverage for “both hospital and physician services.”

Given the wide latitude provided in the Vermont statute, a qualified ICHRA plan provided to your employees would constitute “health care coverage,” so long as it results in payments by your company, as the employer, of any amount, for your employees’ private or public plans that cover “both hospital and physician services.”

Therefore, under Section 2 of the Department’s Health Care Contributions worksheet, Form HC-1, your offer of an ICHRA plan would qualify you as an employer who “offers to pay part or all of the cost of health care coverage” for your employees.

While your ICHRA will qualify as “health care coverage,” you will still owe a Health Care Contribution for “uncovered” employees. These include any employee who is (a) an employee of an employer who does not offer to pay any part of the cost of health care coverage for its employees; or (b) not eligible for the plan you offer; or (c) an employee who is offered the plan but elects not to accept the coverage and is enrolled in Medicaid; has no other health care coverage except Medicaid; or (c) who has purchased health insurance as an individual through the Vermont Health Benefit Exchange. 32 V.S.A. § 10502(7).

To determine whether your employees are “uncovered,” your employees must annually complete Form HC-2, Declaration of Health Care Coverage, and submit it to you.

You may then use the HC-1 worksheet to determine the number of health care contributions for which you may be liable. Your quarterly Health Care Contributions, if any, are reported on Form WHT-436.

General Provisions 

Issuance of this ruling is conditioned upon the understanding that neither the taxpayer nor a related taxpayer is currently under audit or involved in an administrative appeal or litigation concerning the subject matters of the ruling. This ruling is issued solely to the taxpayer and is limited to the facts presented, as affected by current statutes and regulations.

Other taxpayers may refer to this ruling, when redacted to protect confidentiality, to see the Department's general approach, but the Department will not be bound by this ruling in the case of any other taxpayer or in the case of any change in the relevant statutes or regulations.

This ruling will be made public after deletion of the taxpayer’s name and any information which may identify the taxpayer. A copy of this ruling showing the proposed deletions is attached, and you may request within 30 days that the Commissioner delete any further information that might identify the taxpayer. The final discretion as to deletions rests with the Commissioner.

You have the right to appeal this ruling within 30 days. 3 V.S.A. §§ 808, 815.
